If you are looking for a chance to serve others, see the world, and have an adventure unlike any other, you should consider becoming a Seagoing Cowboy. I joined the program expecting hard work and a trip across the ocean, but I gained far more than that. I helped care for animals being sent to people overseas, visited places I had only imagined, and learned that even an ordinary young man can make a meaningful difference in the lives of strangers.

The work was not always easy. On the ship, we had to feed, water, and clean up after the horses and other livestock every day. The animals depended on us, even when the sea was rough, the weather was unpleasant, or we were tired. Still, that responsibility gave our journey a purpose. These animals were not being carried simply as cargo. They were being delivered to families and farmers who needed help rebuilding their lives after the destruction of war. Knowing that a horse or cow might help a family plow a field, grow food, or earn a living made every difficult task worthwhile.

The Seagoing Cowboys program also offered adventures that few people could experience at home. I traveled across the Atlantic Ocean and saw distant ports and unfamiliar countries. Instead of reading about other lands in books, I stood in them myself. I met people with different languages, customs, and ways of life. When we arrived and saw the need in the communities receiving the animals, the trip became more real to me. I understood that people in other nations wanted many of the same things we did: safe homes, enough food, and hope for their children.

Another reason to join is the friendships you make. Life aboard a ship requires cooperation. The cowboys worked side by side, sharing chores, solving problems, and encouraging one another. We came from different backgrounds, but the voyage gave us a common mission. The friendships, the laughter, and even the challenging days made the journey unforgettable.

I would encourage others to become Seagoing Cowboys because the program combines service with discovery. You will work hard, but your work will matter. You will travel far, but you will also grow in understanding. Most important, you will carry hope across the sea to people who need it. For anyone willing to accept responsibility and seek adventure with a purpose, there could be no better voyage.

full_text:
If you are looking for work that offers more than a paycheck, I urge you to become a Seagoing Cowboy. I joined the program expecting an unusual job caring for animals aboard a ship, but I gained far more than an adventure at sea. I traveled to places I had never imagined seeing, met people whose lives had been changed by war, and learned that even an ordinary young person can help rebuild the world.

The Seagoing Cowboys program gave men the chance to escort cattle, horses, and other livestock across the ocean to countries struggling after World War II. These animals were not sent merely as supplies. They represented food, work, and hope. A family that received a cow could have milk for its children and calves to raise or share with neighbors. Farmers who received horses could plow fields again and produce crops. Knowing that my work might help families stand on their own made every difficult day worthwhile.

Life on the ship was certainly not easy. We had to feed the animals, clean their stalls, carry water, and make sure they stayed safe during rough weather. The ocean could be unpredictable, and the ship sometimes rolled so hard that simple chores became exhausting. Still, those challenges taught me responsibility. The animals depended on us, and we had to work together. I formed friendships with other cowboys because we shared the same long hours, jokes, worries, and excitement. We were not just passengers crossing the Atlantic; we were a crew with an important mission.

The best part of the experience came when we reached foreign ports. Visiting countries that had suffered from war showed me how fortunate I had been at home. I saw damaged communities and people working hard to recover. Yet I also saw gratitude and determination. When local families and farmers welcomed the livestock, I understood that our voyage had a purpose beyond travel. The animals we had cared for were now part of someone else’s future.

Of course, joining the program also offers adventure. Few people can say they have ridden the waves of the Atlantic while caring for a shipload of cattle. You may see distant coastlines, explore unfamiliar cities, and hear languages you have never heard before. However, the greatest adventure is discovering that service can take you farther than any map.

I would encourage others to become Seagoing Cowboys because the program combines hard work, travel, friendship, and compassion. You will return with stories to tell, but more importantly, you will return knowing that your efforts helped people rebuild their lives.

Prompt: Your principal is reconsidering the school's cell phone policy. She is considering two possible policies: 
Policy 1: Allow students to bring phones to school and use them during lunch periods and other free times, as long as the phones are turned off during class time. 
Policy 2: Do not allow students to have phones at school at all.
Write a letter to your principal convincing her which policy you believe is better. Support your position with specific reasons.
full_text:
Dear Principal,

I believe the school should adopt Policy 1, allowing students to bring phones to school and use them during lunch and other free times while requiring them to be turned off during class. This policy is more practical, safer, and more respectful of students’ responsibilities than banning phones completely.

First, phones are important tools for communication and safety. Many students arrange rides, after-school activities, jobs, or family responsibilities through their phones. If a practice is canceled, a bus is late, or a family emergency occurs, students need a reliable way to contact parents or guardians. A complete ban could leave students anxious and families unable to reach one another when plans suddenly change. Although the school office can help in emergencies, it cannot provide the same immediate and private communication that a student may need.

Second, allowing phones during free time recognizes that students can use technology responsibly. Lunch and study breaks are not class periods, so using a phone then does not interrupt instruction. Students may listen to music, read, check schedules, communicate with family members, or simply relax with friends. A school policy should teach self-control rather than assume that every student will misuse a device. Requiring phones to be turned off and put away during class establishes a clear boundary: learning comes first, but students still have reasonable freedom when class is not in session.

A total ban would also be difficult to enforce fairly. Students could hide phones in backpacks or pockets, creating unnecessary conflict between students and teachers. Teachers would have to spend valuable time searching for phones or deciding whether someone had violated the rule. Policy 1 is easier to understand and enforce. If a phone rings, is visible, or is used during class, the consequence can be clear and immediate. Because students would be allowed to have phones at appropriate times, they would have less reason to break the rule secretly.

Some people may argue that phones cause distractions, bullying, or cheating. Those concerns are real, but banning phones does not solve them completely. Students can still face bullying online after school, and cheating can be addressed through classroom supervision and reasonable testing procedures. Instead of treating phones as the problem, the school should teach students how to use them responsibly and respectfully.

Policy 1 creates a balanced solution. It protects class time, supports student safety, and gives students the opportunity to demonstrate maturity. I respectfully urge you to allow phones at school while maintaining firm rules against their use during instruction.

Prompt: Your principal is reconsidering the school's cell phone policy. She is considering two possible policies: 
Policy 1: Allow students to bring phones to school and use them during lunch periods and other free times, as long as the phones are turned off during class time. 
Policy 2: Do not allow students to have phones at school at all.
Write a letter to your principal convincing her which policy you believe is better. Support your position with specific reasons.
full_text:
Dear Principal,

I strongly believe that Policy 1, which allows students to bring phones to school but requires them to be turned off during class, is the better choice. This policy protects learning while recognizing that phones can be useful tools for communication, safety, and responsibility. Completely banning phones from school would create unnecessary problems for students, families, and staff.

First, phones are important for safety and transportation. Many students need to contact parents after school because of changing practice times, missed buses, doctor appointments, or unexpected family emergencies. Without phones, students would have to wait in line to use the office phone, and parents might worry if they could not reach their children. In an emergency, a phone can help a student quickly contact a parent or guardian. Although the school office should always remain available, allowing students to carry phones provides an extra layer of security.

Second, Policy 1 teaches students how to use technology responsibly. Phones will be part of students’ lives outside school, in college, and in future jobs. Instead of pretending they do not exist, schools should help students learn when phone use is appropriate and when it is distracting. Requiring phones to be turned off during class sends a clear message: learning comes first. At the same time, allowing phones during lunch and free periods gives students a reasonable amount of independence. Students who follow the rules demonstrate maturity, while students who misuse phones can face consequences.

A complete ban would also be difficult to enforce. Some students might hide phones in backpacks or pockets, making teachers and administrators spend valuable time searching for devices instead of focusing on education. A strict ban could create conflict between students and staff, especially when students need their phones for legitimate reasons. Policy 1 is easier to understand and enforce: phones may be carried, but they may not be used during instruction unless a teacher gives permission for an educational purpose.

Some people may argue that even having phones at school causes distractions. That concern is understandable, since social media, games, and messages can take attention away from class. However, the solution is not to ban every phone. The solution is to establish firm expectations and consequences. Teachers can require phones to remain powered off and put away, and repeated violations can result in the phone being held until the end of the day or picked up by a parent.

Policy 1 creates a fair balance between discipline and practicality. It keeps classrooms focused, helps students stay connected to their families, and teaches responsible behavior. For these reasons, I respectfully urge you to choose Policy 1.

Prompt: Some of your friends perform community service. For example, some tutor elementary school children and others clean up litter. They think helping the community is very important. But other friends of yours think community service takes too much time away from what they need or want to do. 
Your principal is deciding whether to require all students to perform community service. 
Write a letter to your principal in which you take a position on whether students should be required to perform community service. Support your position with examples.
full_text:
Dear Principal,

I believe that all students should be required to complete community service, as long as the school offers a reasonable number of choices and allows students enough time to fulfill the requirement. Community service is not simply extra work; it teaches students responsibility, empathy, and the value of contributing to the place where they live.

First, service helps students understand that their actions can improve other people’s lives. A student who tutors an elementary school child may help that child become more confident in reading or math. The tutor also learns patience and communication skills. Likewise, students who collect litter from parks or sidewalks make their neighborhoods safer and more pleasant for everyone. These projects may seem small, but when many students participate, their combined efforts can make a real difference.

Community service also teaches lessons that cannot always be learned in classrooms. In school, students often focus on grades, tests, and personal goals. Those things are important, but students should also learn to notice the needs of others. For example, volunteering at a food bank could show students how many families struggle to afford groceries. Helping at an animal shelter could teach responsibility and kindness toward animals. Such experiences can help students become more thoughtful citizens as adults.

Some students may argue that service requirements take time away from homework, sports, jobs, or family responsibilities. This concern is understandable. However, the answer should not be to eliminate community service altogether. Instead, the school could require a manageable number of hours each semester and provide flexible opportunities. Students could choose projects that fit their schedules, including weekend events, school-sponsored activities, or service completed during certain class periods. Students with jobs or major family duties could be given additional options or extended deadlines.

A requirement would also be fairer than leaving service entirely voluntary. Students who already care deeply about helping others will probably volunteer anyway, but students who have never tried it may discover an activity they enjoy. Someone who begins volunteering only because it is required might later continue because they feel proud of the results. In this way, the requirement could introduce students to interests and strengths they did not know they had.

For these reasons, I strongly support requiring community service for all students. With flexibility and a variety of opportunities, the program would not be an unfair burden. Instead, it would help students grow into responsible, caring people who understand that a strong community depends on everyone’s willingness to help.

Sincerely,  
A Student

Prompt: Some of your friends perform community service. For example, some tutor elementary school children and others clean up litter. They think helping the community is very important. But other friends of yours think community service takes too much time away from what they need or want to do. 
Your principal is deciding whether to require all students to perform community service. 
Write a letter to your principal in which you take a position on whether students should be required to perform community service. Support your position with examples.
full_text:
Dear Principal,

I strongly believe that students should be required to perform community service. Although some students may worry that volunteering will take time away from homework, sports, jobs, or hobbies, a reasonable service requirement would teach important lessons that cannot be learned only in a classroom. By helping others, students become more responsible, connected to their neighborhoods, and prepared for adult life.

First, community service helps students understand that their actions affect other people. It is easy to walk past litter on a sidewalk or ignore a younger student struggling with reading. However, when students participate in a park cleanup or tutor elementary school children, they see that even a small effort can make a real difference. A student who spends one afternoon collecting trash may help make a playground safer and more welcoming. A student who reads with a child once a week may help that child gain confidence in school. These experiences show students that they have the ability to improve someone else’s day.

Community service also develops useful skills. For example, tutoring requires patience, clear communication, and planning. Working at a food pantry requires organization and teamwork. Volunteering at an animal shelter may teach students how to follow instructions and care for living things. These are skills that will help students in college, careers, and relationships. Employers and colleges often value applicants who have shown that they can work responsibly with others. Therefore, service is not simply time taken away from students’ futures; it can actually help build those futures.

Of course, students have busy schedules, and the school should recognize that. The requirement should be fair and flexible. Instead of demanding many hours every month, the school could require a manageable number of hours over the course of a year. Students should also be allowed to choose from many different activities. Someone who enjoys working with children could tutor, while someone interested in the environment could plant trees or clean up a local river. Students with family responsibilities or jobs could complete service during weekends, school breaks, or through approved projects at school.

Some people argue that volunteering should never be required because service is most meaningful when it is voluntary. While that is partly true, many students may never try community service unless they are encouraged to do so. Once they begin, they may discover causes they care about and continue helping even after completing the requirement. A required first step can lead to a lifelong habit of generosity.

For these reasons, I hope you will require community service while giving students choices and reasonable deadlines. Our school would not only produce successful students, but also caring citizens who are ready to strengthen the community around them.

Sincerely,  
A Concerned Student

Schools should offer distance learning as an option because it can make education more accessible, flexible, and effective for many students. Although learning from home cannot replace every benefit of a traditional classroom, students who have the choice to attend online classes can continue their education during difficult circumstances and work in ways that better fit their needs.

First, distance learning helps students who cannot always travel to school. A student with a chronic illness, a temporary injury, or a weakened immune system may miss many classes simply because attending in person is unsafe or exhausting. Similarly, students who live far from school or have unreliable transportation may spend hours commuting each week. Online instruction allows these students to participate in lessons, ask questions, and submit assignments without losing valuable instructional time. Rather than falling behind because of circumstances beyond their control, they can remain connected to their teachers and classmates.

Distance learning can also encourage students to become more independent. In a traditional classroom, teachers often remind students about every deadline and guide them through each activity. At home, however, students must organize their schedules, check online materials, and take responsibility for completing work. These habits are useful beyond school. College courses, jobs, and adult responsibilities all require people to manage time and communicate clearly without constant supervision. For example, a student who learns to use a digital calendar to track assignments may later use the same skill to balance college classes and part-time work.

In addition, online classes can provide learning tools that are difficult to use in a regular classroom. Recorded lessons allow students to review challenging explanations, pause a lecture, or replay an important section before a test. Digital discussion boards may also give quieter students a chance to express ideas that they would be too nervous to share aloud. A student who struggles with a fast-paced math lesson, for instance, can rewatch the teacher’s example and practice at a comfortable speed.

Critics rightly point out that students may feel isolated at home or become distracted by phones, games, and family responsibilities. These concerns are real, especially for younger students. However, they do not mean that distance learning should be rejected entirely. Schools can require live video sessions, provide regular teacher check-ins, create virtual group projects, and offer counseling or tutoring. Most importantly, online learning should be an option rather than a requirement for everyone.

By giving students the ability to attend classes from home, schools can remove barriers that prevent many young people from succeeding. When it is carefully organized and supported, distance learning expands educational opportunity while teaching skills that students will need throughout their lives.

Prompt: Some schools offer distance learning as an option for students to attend classes from home by way of online or video conferencing. Do you think students would benefit from being able to attend classes from home? Take a position on this issue. Support your response with reasons and examples.
full_text:
Students would benefit from having the option to attend classes from home, although distance learning should not completely replace traditional schools. Online instruction can make education more accessible, flexible, and resilient, especially for students whose circumstances make daily attendance difficult. When schools provide well-designed virtual classes, they give more students a fair opportunity to learn.

First, attending from home can help students with health problems, disabilities, or family responsibilities. A student recovering from surgery, for example, may be physically unable to travel to school but still capable of listening to lessons and completing assignments online. Without a distance-learning option, that student could fall behind for weeks. Similarly, students with chronic illnesses may miss many days of school because of medical appointments or fatigue. Video conferencing allows them to remain connected to teachers and classmates without risking their health. Rather than treating absence as an unavoidable barrier, schools can use technology to keep learning continuous.

Distance learning can also improve access for students who live far from school or face transportation problems. In rural areas, some students spend hours each day riding buses. Bad weather, unreliable transportation, or family schedules can make attendance even more difficult. Online classes would reduce wasted travel time and allow students to use that time for studying, resting, or participating in extracurricular activities. For older students who work part-time or help care for younger siblings, a remote option can make it possible to balance responsibilities without abandoning their education.

In addition, learning from home can teach valuable independent skills. Students in virtual classes must manage deadlines, communicate clearly through email or discussion boards, and organize their work without constant reminders. These habits are useful in college and in many modern workplaces, where employees often collaborate online. A motivated student might watch a recorded science lesson, pause to review a difficult idea, and then ask questions during a virtual meeting. This level of control can help some learners understand material more deeply than they would in a fast-moving classroom.

Critics correctly argue that students need social interaction and that some homes do not provide quiet spaces or reliable internet. For this reason, distance learning should be an option rather than a requirement. Schools should continue offering in-person instruction, provide devices and internet support when possible, and schedule opportunities for online students to meet teachers and peers. With these safeguards, virtual learning can complement—not weaken—the school community.

Giving students the choice to attend classes from home recognizes that they do not all face the same circumstances. A flexible education system can protect health, reduce barriers, and prepare students for the digital world while still preserving the benefits of classroom learning.

Students would benefit from having the option to attend classes from home, provided that schools design online learning carefully and do not treat it as a complete replacement for the classroom. Distance learning can give students greater flexibility, protect their health, and allow them to learn in environments where they can focus. Although in-person school remains valuable, a home-based option would make education more accessible to many students.

First, remote attendance can help students whose personal circumstances make daily travel to school difficult. A student who lives far from campus may spend hours each day on a bus or in a car. That time could instead be used for sleep, homework, exercise, or family responsibilities. Students with temporary illnesses or injuries would also be able to keep up with lessons without exposing classmates to contagious diseases. For example, a student recovering from surgery may be physically unable to walk through crowded hallways but still capable of listening to a lecture and completing assignments online. Without a distance-learning option, that student might fall behind simply because getting to school is difficult.

Learning from home can also improve concentration for some students. Traditional classrooms can be noisy, crowded, and stressful. A student who is easily distracted may learn more effectively in a quiet room with headphones and fewer interruptions. Online platforms often allow teachers to record lessons, share notes digitally, and post assignments in one place. If a student does not understand a math problem or misses an important point in a history lecture, that student can review the material rather than relying only on memory. This ability to pause, replay, and revisit lessons encourages students to take more responsibility for their education.

Critics may argue that students need school to socialize and develop communication skills. This concern is reasonable, because friendships, group projects, sports, and clubs are important parts of growing up. However, offering remote learning as an option does not mean eliminating those opportunities. Schools could allow online students to attend extracurricular activities, participate in scheduled discussion sessions, or come to campus for labs and presentations. Video conferences can also include small-group work, debates, and teacher conferences. The goal should be flexibility, not isolation.

Of course, distance learning will only succeed if schools provide reliable technology, clear schedules, and regular support from teachers. Students without internet access or quiet study spaces should be given devices, hotspots, or access to supervised learning centers. With these safeguards, attending classes from home can help more students remain engaged, healthy, and successful.

The Electoral College was created when travel, communication, and voting access were very different from today. Although it was intended to balance the interests of states, it can now produce results that conflict with the will of the majority.

Under the current system, each state receives electoral votes based partly on its population and partly on its number of senators. This gives smaller states more influence per voter than larger states. For example, a voter in a sparsely populated state may have more impact on the outcome than a voter in a heavily populated state. More importantly, most states award all of their electoral votes to the candidate who wins the state by even a tiny margin. I respectfully ask you to support reforms, including the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact or a constitutional amendment, that would ensure the presidency goes to the candidate chosen by the most Americans.

Sincerely,

A Concerned Constituent

I urge you to support changing presidential elections to a national popular vote. The principle of representative government is simple: every citizen’s vote should carry equal weight. Under the current Electoral College system, however, a candidate can win the presidency while receiving fewer votes nationwide than an opponent. Although this outcome is rare, it has happened more than once in American history, showing that the system can conflict with the idea that the candidate preferred by the most voters should lead the country.

Supporters of the Electoral College argue that it protects smaller states and prevents candidates from focusing only on large cities. They also note that the system reflects the Constitution’s federal structure, since states play an important role in national government. These concerns deserve respect. Smaller states should not be ignored, and rural communities should have a voice in presidential elections. Yet the Electoral College does not truly guarantee attention to every small state. Instead, candidates concentrate on a limited number of competitive “swing states,” whether those states are large or small. Voters in states that reliably support one party often receive fewer campaign visits, advertisements, and policy promises because their electoral votes are considered predictable.

A national popular vote would encourage candidates to seek support everywhere. A Republican voter in a heavily Democratic state and a Democratic voter in a heavily Republican state would both have a reason to participate, because every vote would add to the national total. At present, many citizens feel their votes do not matter because the outcome in their state seems certain. Election results and voter-participation research have repeatedly shown that close contests motivate people to vote. Making every ballot equally valuable could strengthen participation and public confidence.

Another concern is that a popular-vote system could create difficult nationwide recounts. However, recounts are generally necessary only when results are extremely close. Modern election procedures already involve local counting, audits, and recount rules, which could continue under a national system. In contrast, the Electoral College can make a tiny number of votes in one closely divided state determine the entire presidency, even when millions more people voted elsewhere. That situation can produce just as much uncertainty while making the final outcome seem less fair.

The Electoral College was created in a different era, when communication was slow, voting rights were limited, and citizens had far less direct involvement in government. Our nation has expanded democracy since then by ending many restrictions on voting and by allowing citizens to elect senators directly. Choosing the president by popular vote would continue that democratic progress.

Please work with other state leaders to support reform that ensures every American vote counts equally. The presidency belongs to the whole nation, and the candidate chosen by the greatest number of voters should serve it.

Sincerely,  
A Concerned Constituent

Because the presidency represents the entire nation, every citizen’s vote should carry the same weight, regardless of the state in which that citizen lives.

One major advantage of driverless cars is safety. Human drivers can become distracted by phones, tired after long workdays, or impaired by alcohol and drugs. They may speed, ignore traffic signs, or make poor decisions in dangerous weather. A driverless vehicle, however, can use cameras, sensors, maps, and computer programs to monitor the road constantly. It does not get sleepy or look away from traffic. As the article suggests, automated cars could reduce crashes caused by human error. Even if self-driving systems are not perfect, they may eventually be safer than ordinary drivers if they are tested carefully and required to meet high safety standards.

Driverless cars could also help people who cannot easily drive themselves. Elderly people, people with disabilities, and individuals with medical conditions often depend on relatives, public transportation, or expensive rides to get to school, work, appointments, and stores. A reliable autonomous vehicle could give these people greater independence. For example, a person with limited vision might be able to travel without needing someone else to drive. This increased freedom could improve many people’s quality of life.

Instead of drivers braking suddenly or causing traffic jams, automated cars might move more smoothly through intersections and highways. Although people have valid concerns about trusting computers with such an important responsibility, the dangers of human driving are already severe. With careful testing, strong safety rules, and human oversight during the transition, self-driving vehicles could improve life for many people.

One of the strongest arguments for driverless cars is that they could reduce accidents caused by human error. Drivers become distracted by phones, tired after long workdays, angry in traffic, or impaired by alcohol and drugs. A computer does not text, fall asleep, or lose its temper. Driverless cars can use cameras, sensors, radar, and detailed maps to watch the road in every direction at once. They may be able to react faster than a person when another car suddenly stops or when a pedestrian enters the street. Since traffic crashes injure and kill many people each year, technology that can prevent even some of those accidents deserves serious development.

Driverless cars could also help people who cannot easily drive themselves. Older adults, people with disabilities, and people with medical conditions may have difficulty getting to work, school, appointments, or stores. A reliable autonomous vehicle could give these individuals more independence instead of forcing them to depend on relatives, buses, or expensive taxi rides. In addition, self-driving vehicles could make travel more efficient. If cars communicate with one another and choose safer routes, they could reduce traffic jams, save fuel, and possibly lower pollution from vehicles sitting idle on crowded roads.

However, opponents are right to worry about problems such as computer failures, hacking, and confusing ethical decisions during emergencies. A sensor could malfunction in bad weather, or software might not correctly recognize a construction zone or a cyclist. There is also the difficult question of who is responsible if a driverless car causes a crash: the passenger, the car company, or the software designer? These risks show that driverless cars should not simply be released without limits. Companies must test them in many different situations, governments must create clear safety standards, and humans should remain able to take control when necessary.

Some people may also fear that driverless technology will eliminate jobs for taxi, delivery, and truck drivers. This concern should be taken seriously, and communities should provide training for workers whose jobs change. Still, the possibility of job disruption is not a reason to reject a technology that could save lives. Instead, society should prepare workers for new transportation and technology-related careers.

In conclusion, driverless cars offer more benefits than drawbacks when they are developed responsibly. They could prevent accidents, assist people with limited mobility, and improve traffic flow. The technology must be carefully regulated, but refusing to develop it would ignore an opportunity to make roads safer for everyone.

Dear Principal,

I strongly oppose requiring students to maintain at least a B average in order to participate in sports and other school activities. Students with C averages should be supported, not excluded from the very programs that keep them motivated and connected to school.

That success can build confidence and make the student more willing to ask for help with schoolwork. If students are removed from activities because of a C average, they may feel discouraged and decide that school is not a place where they can succeed. Rather than improving their grades, they could become less interested in attending school or completing assignments.

Second, a C average does not mean that a student is lazy or unconcerned about education. Some students have learning differences, family responsibilities, jobs, health problems, or difficult classes that affect their grades. For example, a student taking advanced science and math courses may earn several Cs while working extremely hard, while another student in less demanding courses may have a B average more easily. A single grade average cannot show how much effort, improvement, or responsibility a student demonstrates.

Sports and activities also teach valuable skills that cannot always be learned in the classroom. Team members learn cooperation, leadership, time management, discipline, and perseverance. Students in theater learn public speaking and confidence. Members of clubs develop friendships and a sense of belonging. These experiences can help students become more responsible, which may eventually lead to better grades. Taking them away would remove an important source of growth.

Instead of setting a strict B-average requirement, the school could create a more reasonable policy. Students with low grades could be required to attend tutoring, meet regularly with teachers, complete missing work, or show improvement during each grading period. This approach would hold students accountable while allowing them to remain involved in positive activities. Coaches and club advisers could also check on students’ progress and encourage them to use study halls or academic support programs.

Requiring a B average would punish many hardworking students and could push them away from school. A policy focused on improvement, support, and accountability would be fairer and more effective.

Sincerely,

A Concerned Student

Our school should encourage students to succeed both academically and personally. Keeping activities available to students with C averages would give them motivation, support, and a chance to grow. Rather than excluding them, we should help them improve.

Prompt: Your principal has decided that all students must participate in at least one extracurricular activity. For example, students could participate in sports, work on the yearbook, or serve on the student council. Do you agree or disagree with this decision? Use specific details and examples to convince others to support your position.
full_text:
I agree that every student should participate in at least one extracurricular activity because these activities teach lessons that cannot be learned fully in a classroom. Sports teams, clubs, student government, theater, music, and school publications give students opportunities to discover their strengths, build relationships, and develop responsibility. Although students should be allowed to choose an activity that fits their interests and schedules, requiring some form of participation would make school a more supportive and successful community.

First, extracurricular activities help students feel connected to school. A student who only attends classes may see school as a place to complete assignments and take tests. In contrast, a student who joins the robotics club or plays on the soccer team has a reason to stay after school, meet people with similar interests, and take pride in the school’s accomplishments. This connection can be especially important for new or shy students. For example, a student who struggles to make friends in a large cafeteria may feel more comfortable talking with classmates while designing a yearbook page or rehearsing for a play. One activity can turn a lonely school experience into a welcoming one.

Extracurricular activities also teach practical skills that employers and colleges value. A student council member must communicate clearly, plan events, and work with people who have different opinions. A member of the debate team learns to research evidence and speak confidently in front of others. Athletes learn discipline because they must attend practice, follow instructions, and continue working even after a disappointing loss. These experiences prepare students for adulthood, where success often depends on cooperation, persistence, and leadership rather than test scores alone.

Some people may argue that a requirement would place too much pressure on busy students. That concern is reasonable, especially for students who have jobs, family responsibilities, or transportation difficulties. However, the policy does not have to require hours of activity every day. Schools could offer flexible options, including lunchtime clubs, short-term service projects, online publication work, or activities that meet only once a week. Students who work or care for siblings could receive accommodations or choose activities connected to those responsibilities, such as volunteering at a school event on a weekend.

Most importantly, requiring participation would encourage students to try opportunities they might otherwise avoid. Many students are nervous about joining a club because they fear they will not fit in or will not be talented enough. A requirement could give them the small push they need to take a chance. They may discover a talent for photography, leadership, coding, or music that they never knew they had.

School should prepare students not only to pass classes, but also to participate confidently in their communities. Requiring one extracurricular activity, while allowing flexible choices, would help every student grow beyond the classroom.

full_text:
Although extracurricular activities can enrich school life, requiring every student to join one is an unfair policy. Schools should encourage students to participate in sports, clubs, service projects, and student government, but participation should remain a choice. Students have different responsibilities, interests, and needs outside the classroom, and a mandatory activity could create stress rather than build character.

First, many students already have important commitments after school. Some care for younger siblings while their parents work. Others have part-time jobs to help pay for clothes, transportation, or family expenses. For example, a student who works at a grocery store four afternoons a week may need that income more than a position on the yearbook staff. If the school forces that student to attend club meetings, the student might have to reduce work hours or lose sleep trying to complete everything. A policy meant to create opportunities should not punish students for supporting their families.

In addition, students benefit most from activities they genuinely choose. A person who loves drawing may devote energy to the art club, while someone interested in public issues may enjoy student council. However, a student forced to join a club simply to meet a requirement may attend without enthusiasm, contribute very little, and make extra work for the other members. On a sports team, for instance, an unwilling player may skip practices or resent the commitment. This does not help the team, the coach, or the student. True involvement comes from interest, not from a rule.

Mandatory extracurricular participation could also harm students who need time to focus on academics or mental health. High school classes can be demanding, especially for students taking advanced courses or struggling in a particular subject. Some students need afternoons for tutoring, homework, or quiet rest. If they are required to add a club meeting or practice to their schedules, they may become overwhelmed. Schools often tell students to balance their responsibilities, yet this policy would remove their ability to make that balance for themselves.

Instead of making activities compulsory, the principal should make them more accessible and appealing. The school could hold a club fair, provide late buses, allow students to start new organizations, and recognize participation with awards or course credit. Teachers could also explain how activities help students make friends, develop leadership skills, and explore careers. These approaches would invite students to participate without forcing them.

Extracurricular activities are valuable, but their value depends on voluntary commitment. By encouraging rather than requiring participation, the school can respect students’ different lives while still creating a stronger, more active community.

Cell phones have become essential tools for communication, navigation, and work, but their convenience does not outweigh the responsibility drivers have to protect passengers, pedestrians, cyclists, and other motorists. A moving vehicle requires constant attention, and a driver who divides that attention between the road and a phone creates an unnecessary danger.

Many people assume that hands-free calling or voice-controlled texting is safe because the driver’s hands remain on the steering wheel. However, distraction is not limited to taking one’s eyes off the road. A phone conversation requires mental focus: the driver listens, responds, thinks about what to say, and may become emotionally involved in the discussion. This mental distraction can delay reaction time just as surely as looking down at a screen. A driver may fail to notice a child entering a crosswalk, a car braking suddenly, or a traffic light changing because his or her mind is focused on the phone rather than the roadway.

Texting and scrolling are even more hazardous. Reading a message for only a few seconds may seem harmless, but at highway speeds, a vehicle can travel the length of a football field during that short glance. In that distance, conditions can change completely. Traffic can stop, an animal can enter the road, or another driver can make an unexpected mistake. Because safe driving depends on anticipating hazards, drivers cannot afford to surrender even a few seconds of visual attention.

Some people argue that phones are necessary for GPS directions or urgent communication. Navigation can be useful, but drivers should set directions before beginning a trip and pull over safely if changes are needed. Likewise, a person facing an emergency should stop the vehicle before making a call whenever possible. Emergency situations do not justify routine phone use, and laws can include reasonable exceptions for reporting immediate danger when stopping is impossible. These limited exceptions should not become excuses for everyday distractions.

A complete ban on cell phone use while driving would also make expectations clearer. Laws that prohibit only texting or handheld calls can be difficult to enforce and may encourage drivers to believe other forms of phone use are harmless. A simple rule—drive first, use the phone only after parking—would be easier to understand and would promote a stronger culture of responsibility.

Operating a vehicle is a privilege that demands full concentration. No message, call, social media post, or app notification is worth risking a life. Drivers should therefore be prohibited from using cell phones while operating a vehicle, except in the rarest emergencies, because safety must remain more important than convenience.

Prompt: Today the majority of humans own and operate cell phones on a daily basis. In essay form, explain if drivers should or should not be able to use cell phones in any capacity while operating a vehicle.
full_text:
Drivers should not be able to use cell phones in any capacity while operating a vehicle because safe driving requires continuous attention, quick judgment, and full awareness of the road. Although cell phones have become essential tools for communication, navigation, and emergencies, their convenience does not outweigh the danger created when a driver divides attention between a screen, a conversation, and traffic. A vehicle can travel hundreds of feet in only a few seconds, meaning even a brief distraction can have permanent consequences.

Many people recognize that texting while driving is dangerous, yet they often believe that hands-free calling, voice commands, or glancing at a navigation app are harmless alternatives. However, the primary problem is not simply holding a phone. It is mental distraction. When drivers participate in a phone conversation, listen to messages, or dictate a response, part of their attention leaves the road. They may look directly ahead but fail to notice a pedestrian entering a crosswalk, a car slowing suddenly, or a traffic light changing. Driving safely depends not only on seeing hazards but also on processing them quickly enough to react.

Cell phone use also encourages overconfidence. Drivers may assume that they can multitask because they have used their phones behind the wheel before without causing an accident. Yet avoiding a crash in the past does not prove that the behavior is safe; it may simply mean that no unexpected hazard occurred at the wrong moment. A child chasing a ball into the street, a cyclist swerving around debris, or a driver braking suddenly can turn a small lapse in attention into a serious collision. Because roads are unpredictable, drivers must prepare for situations that demand immediate concentration.

Some people argue that phones are necessary for navigation or emergency communication. These needs can be addressed without allowing active phone use while the vehicle is moving. Drivers can set their destination before leaving, place the phone out of reach, and pull over safely if directions need to be changed. In an emergency, stopping in a parking lot, on a shoulder when appropriate, or at another safe location is far better than risking another emergency through distraction. Modern cars can also provide built-in navigation systems that limit interaction while driving.

Ultimately, operating a vehicle is a responsibility, not a time for constant connection. Laws should prohibit drivers from using cell phones in any capacity while a vehicle is in motion, including hands-free conversations and voice messaging. A missed call or delayed reply is temporary, but a distracted-driving crash can cause injuries, deaths, and lifelong regret.

Although too many opinions can occasionally feel confusing, carefully comparing advice usually gives a person a clearer and more realistic understanding of a situation.

First, each adviser brings unique experiences and knowledge. A student deciding whether to attend a nearby college or a university far from home, for example, might ask a teacher, a parent, and an older friend. The teacher may focus on academic programs and internship opportunities. A parent may raise practical questions about tuition, housing, and transportation. Meanwhile, the older friend may describe what daily life on a campus actually feels like, including the challenge of making friends or managing time independently. Multiple opinions also protect people from relying too heavily on one person’s bias. Even well-meaning advisers can be influenced by their own preferences. A parent who loved living close to family might strongly encourage a child to choose a local school, while a friend who enjoyed studying abroad might insist that leaving home is always best. full_text:
The “Face on Mars” may look mysterious at first, but the best scientific evidence shows that it is a natural landform, not a monument built by aliens. People began calling it a face after a photograph taken by the Viking spacecraft showed what seemed to be eyes, a nose, and a mouth on a hill in the Cydonia region of Mars. However, scientists must examine more than one unusual picture before deciding what it means. When later spacecraft photographed the same area more clearly, the supposed face was revealed to be an ordinary rocky mesa shaped by erosion, shadows, and chance.

One important reason to believe the Face is natural is that its appearance changes depending on the angle of sunlight. In the original Viking image, sunlight came from one side of the hill. This lighting created dark shadows that resembled eye sockets and a mouth, while brighter areas looked like a nose and forehead. The article explains that low-resolution images can make surface features seem more regular or artificial than they really are. Human beings are especially likely to recognize familiar patterns, including faces, even when no face was intended. This tendency, sometimes called seeing patterns where none exist, explains why the formation seemed so convincing in the first photograph.

Later images provided stronger evidence. Higher-resolution photographs from later Mars missions showed that the “Face” has an uneven surface covered with ridges, slopes, craters, and rocks. Instead of smooth, carefully carved features, the landform has the rough, irregular texture expected from a natural hill. From different viewing angles, the face-like features nearly disappear. If aliens had constructed a giant sculpture, its eyes, nose, and mouth would remain clear regardless of the direction of sunlight or the position of a camera. The fact that the image looks face-like only under certain conditions supports the conclusion that light and shadow created the illusion.

The surrounding landscape also supports a natural explanation. Mars has many mesas, hills, craters, and cliffs formed by impacts, wind erosion, landslides, and the wearing away of ancient rock layers. The Face is consistent with these other Martian landforms. Scientists have found no evidence of building materials, straight walls, machinery, roads, or other structures that would suggest intelligent construction. Extraordinary claims, such as alien architects, require extraordinary evidence. A blurry image is not enough to outweigh the detailed observations from multiple spacecraft.

In conclusion, the Face on Mars is interesting because it reminds people how easily images can fool us. Yet careful scientific investigation shows that it is a naturally eroded hill whose shadows briefly create the appearance of a human face. Rather than proving aliens visited Mars, the formation demonstrates why scientists rely on repeated observations, clearer images, and evidence instead of first impressions.
